1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop to contest the long diagonal, where the fight for e4 and d5 is decided. White gives up a quick e3 and Bd3 in return for a safe king and lasting pressure from a distance, a slower, positional game against Black's own fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and prepares a pawn on e4, but leaves Black the choice: the quiet bishop on the long diagonal, or a pin on the knight that steers toward doubled pawns. White accepts that choice for the chance to build a big centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Petrosian Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3.background: Garry Kasparov often used it early in his career.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3.strategy: Takes b4 away from Black's bishop, so the knight can come to c3 without being pinned, and prepares a big pawn centre. The a-pawn move costs time and invites Black to fight for e4 with pieces, so White's centre has to be built against resistance.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Spassky System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3.strategy: A modest, flexible development that opens the diagonal for the king's bishop and prepares to castle early. It does not fight for e4 as sharply as the fianchetto, so the game tends toward complex manoeuvring rather than an immediate clash in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Bf4.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Miles Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Bf4.background: Tony Miles had some success with the line, but it has never been popular.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Bf4.strategy: Brings the bishop out to a good square outside the pawn chain, a simple, safe set-up. But it does little against Black's grip on e4 and leaves the centre unchallenged, so Black can develop in comfort.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal, where with the f6 knight it controls e4, the square White's plan needs. Black accepts a slower game against White's expanding pawns and relies on the pressure on e4 to hold the centre together.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Ba6.strategy: Attacks the c4 pawn, which has no defender yet, and makes White spend time or loosen the set-up to hold it. Black swaps pressure on e4 for pressure on c4, which makes the extra move a3 look less useful than it did.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and discourages a broad pawn centre. If White pushes the pawn to d5, the bishop swings to a6 and attacks c4, which has no defender, and a3 has done little to help. Black accepts a less natural development order for active counterplay.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Ba6 5.Qc2.strategy: Defends c4 with the queen, so the attack of the bishop leads nowhere, and puts it on the diagonal toward e4 and h7 without blocking any piece. The cost is a queen committed early and a bishop on a6 that stays active.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Ba6 5.Nbd.strategy: Defends c4 with a developing move, but the knight blocks the queen's support of d4 and the bishop on c1, so Black can strike at the centre with the c-pawn at once. Sound, but it hands Black the initiative.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Ba6 5.Qa4.strategy: Guards c4 along the fourth rank and eyes the bishop on a6, which the b8 knight defends. The queen leaves the centre for the edge of the board, where it does little for the fight over d4. A playable but awkward way to hold the pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Ba6 5.Qc2.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Petrosian Variation, Farago Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Ba6 5.Qc2.strategy: Brings the bishop back to the long diagonal now that White has committed the queen to c2: the sortie to a6 has provoked a defensive queen move, and bishop and knight again pressure e4. Black prepares to strike at the centre with the c-pawn in a game where White has spent time on a3 and Qc2.
Strikes at d4 immediately, but without the bishop on the long diagonal White's central advance meets less resistance and can gain space. Sound, but it lets White decide how the centre is resolved.

A neutral developing move that prepares castling and waits. The bishop on a6 stays where it is and Black has not yet decided how to challenge the centre, so White gets time to develop the knight and build in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.background: By the mid-1980s the more common way to reach it was 4.Nc3 Bb7 5.a3, which spares White the replies 4.a3 c5 5.d5 and 4.a3 Ba6.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Completes the plan that a3 began: the knight develops with no fear of a pin and prepares to build a broad centre. Black's bishop and knight both watch e4, so White gains space only if Black's control of that square is overcome.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Bg5.strategy: Pins the knight against the queen to loosen Black's grip on e4 and d5. It develops a piece, but the knight on c3, which the move a3 was meant to prepare, is still missing, and Black can ask the bishop to decide at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.e3.strategy: Solid but unambitious: it supports d4 and frees the bishop, yet gives up the plan of a quick pawn centre that a3 prepared. Black has time to take a share of the centre and equalise.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation, Main Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Meets White's plan by putting a pawn on d5, which attacks c4 and takes e4 away. The tension between the c4 and d5 pawns decides the game's character, and Black bets on the pieces behind the pawn, with the bishop's diagonal, to equalise in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation, Andersson Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Plants the knight on e4 before White can put a pawn there, and attacks the c3 knight at once. Trades ease Black's position, and a recapture with the b-pawn would double White's pawns. The knight on e4 is also a target, and White gains time to build.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation, Marco Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: A flexible waiting move: the bishop develops, castling is prepared, and the knight and bishop keep watching e4. Black commits to no central break yet and lets White show how the centre will be built, reacting to it from a solid position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation, Hedgehog Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Prepares a second fianchetto, so Black's pieces will use both long diagonals. Black stays compact and flexible, but the pawn move does nothing about the centre, which White can occupy once e4 is prepared; the bishop on g7 is a long-term counter to it.

Takes away the pawn that was holding back e4 and half-opens the c-file for White. Black must recapture, and the choice of recapture sets the pawn structure of the middlegame, with White's central push now a real threat that Black has to take seriously.

Pins the f6 knight to the queen to raise the pressure on d5 and e4 before the centre is clarified. It lets Black take the c4 pawn, and White must then find its compensation in quick development, so the initiative shifts to Black.

Quiet and solid: it supports d4 and opens the bishop but does nothing about the tension on c4 and d5. Black can take on c4 or hold the centre as it likes, and White's space advantage disappears. Playable, but short of ambition.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation, Modern Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, keeping the e-pawn at home, so no pawn blocks the b7 bishop's diagonal. The knight on d5 invites trades that relieve Black's lack of space, and White tries to dislodge it with a central pawn push while Black relies on piece activity.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Kasparov-Petrosian Variation, Classical Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.a3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn for a firm pawn on d5 and an open e-file. The price is that the d5 pawn blocks the b7 bishop's diagonal, so Black gets a solid centre but a passive bishop, and plays against White's queenside majority.

Recaptures with the bishop and gives up the piece that eyes e4 from the long diagonal. White trades it off with Nxd5, and e4 then hits the knight that retakes with tempo, so White gets the broad centre the Queen's Indian was meant to prevent.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Spassky System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal, which together with the f6 knight keeps e4 under watch. Black answers the quiet move in kind, with a solid set-up that leaves White's centre without a good break and prepares to castle.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 straight away, so White cannot build the centre in peace. The bishop can still go to the long diagonal afterwards. If White resolves the tension, the c-file opens for Black; if not, the pressure on d4 forces White to commit.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn and covers e4. The cost lies in the bishop: with the b-pawn already on b6, a recapture with the e-pawn on d5 blocks the long diagonal, so the fianchetto loses much of its point.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Spassky System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop toward the kingside, where it supports a pawn on e4 and looks at h7, and prepares to castle. The set-up is solid and unhurried, and it keeps White's central tension for later rather than committing the pawns now.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to fight for d5 and e4, accepting that Black may pin it with the dark-squared bishop. White keeps its pieces flexible and aims for a central break, while Black counters by keeping e4 under watch.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Be2.strategy: A modest alternative to the active bishop on d3: it prepares castling and keeps the structure compact, but it is less active, since it neither supports e4 nor aims at h7. Solid and harmless, with a little less pressure on Black.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Spassky System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn, which controls e4 and stops White's pawn centre. Black accepts a slightly cramped but solid chain and relies on easy development and later pressure on the c4 pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Spassky System3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, so White cannot finish development at leisure. If White allows the exchange, the c-file opens and Black's pieces gain activity; the early pawn move means Black gives up a little of the solid structure for the fight.

Develops the bishop and prepares castling while the pawn structure stays flexible. Black delays the fight for the centre and relies on the knight and bishop to control e4. The position stays solid, with Black reacting to White's plan rather than setting it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.strategy: Castles and completes the quiet development, keeping the central tension. White waits for Black to clarify the c-pawn before choosing a plan: the king is safe, and the bishop on d3 already points at Black's kingside.

Develops the knight rather than castling, adding pressure on the centre and keeping the option of a pawn push in the middle. The king stays in the centre a move longer, and White invites Black to resolve the tension on d4.

Gives up the central pawn: Black recaptures with the bishop or the b-pawn and develops with ease, while White has traded the pawn that held the centre and has no clear follow-up. Sound but unambitious.
Resolves the tension at once: Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens the c-file. White recaptures and keeps a broad centre, while Black's pieces become more active.

Adds a second attacker against d4 and develops a piece in the centre, keeping the choice of how to resolve the tension. White must decide about castling and the centre, while Black's pieces become active before the pawn structure is fixed.

Challenges the centre at once with the second central pawn. After the exchanges the pawns on c5 and d5 stand side by side and control much space, but they can become targets if White blockades them. Playable but double-edged.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop toward castling and keeps the position solid while the pressure on d4 and e4 stays. A standard, flexible move: Black delays any decision about the centre, and White decides how the tension is resolved.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.e3 Bb7 5.Bd3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the second bishop and shuts the white bishop's diagonal toward h7. It costs time compared with simple development and commits the king's side to a less flexible set-up than the usual one, for a bishop that does not yet have a clear target.

Resolves the tension: White takes back with a pawn and holds the centre, while Black gets the open c-file and free play for the pieces. The price is a strong pawn centre that Black has to play against.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 Bb7.strategy: The natural development: the bishop completes the fianchetto and fights for the e4 and d5 squares from a distance, and Black keeps the option of pinning the c3 knight with the dark-squared bishop. White decides how sharp the game becomes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the c3 knight against the king and threatens to double White's pawns with ...Bxc3+, while the b6 fianchetto keeps a grip on e4. Black mixes two set-ups, and White must find a way to meet the pin without losing the plans for the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn at once, giving up the Indian plan of controlling it from a distance. The pawn on d5 blocks the long diagonal of the b7-bishop to come, so the fianchetto loses much of its point.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 Bb7 5.a3.strategy: Prevents ...Bb4, so the c3 knight cannot be pinned and White can go ahead with a broad pawn centre. Black answers by fighting for e4 and d5 with pieces, and a rich strategic fight follows.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 Bb7 5.Bg.strategy: An older line: the bishop pins the f6 knight against the queen and asks Black to decide how to meet it. Black gets good equalising chances, so White gets little out of the pin, but the position stays tense and rich in ideas.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 Bb7 5.e3.strategy: A quiet developing move: it supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop, but lets Black decide the character of the game, by pinning the knight or by striking in the centre. White gets a sound, flexible position without pressing for an advantage.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 Bb7 5.Bg.strategy: Asks the bishop what it wants: retreat and keep the pin, or exchange on f6. The pawn move costs a tempo but forces White to declare itself, and Black keeps a flexible structure with the bishop on b7 ready to fight for e4 and d5.

Breaks the pin by putting the bishop behind the knight, and prepares to castle. Black keeps the pawn structure intact and avoids the kingside weakening that a pawn thrust brings, at the price of a solid but slightly passive position.

Counter-pins the c3 knight against the king, so each side has a pinned knight and the position stays tense. Black accepts that the bishop may be traded for the knight, which doubles White's pawns if White recaptures, in return for pressure on the centre.

Keeps the pin and the bishop rather than exchanging on f6, and makes Black solve the pin. Black's natural counter, a pawn advance on the kingside, weakens the king's cover, which is the trade-off of the whole line.

Takes the knight and settles the question of the bishop's future, but hands Black the pair of bishops. The queen recaptures early, yet the two bishops compensate; sound, but it gives Black a comfortable game.
Moves the bishop out of the pin to f4, where it eyes c7 and the d6 square and keeps the bishop pair. The bishop can be hit again by a kingside pawn advance, so the move gains little.

Challenges the bishop and takes the sting out of the pin at once: the bishop has to retreat, and Black can then trade it off by attacking it with the f6 knight. The cost is a weakened kingside, where Black's king will rarely feel entirely safe.

Pins the c3 knight against the king instead of reacting on the kingside, so both sides have a pinned knight and the position stays tense. Black keeps the kingside pawns where they are, at the price of leaving the f6 knight pinned against the queen.

Unpins by developing the bishop behind the knight and prepares to castle. White can trade on f6, after which Black keeps the pair of bishops but White gets a free hand in the centre; a solid, slightly passive choice.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 d5 5.cxd.strategy: Clarifies the centre by exchanging the c-pawn for Black's d-pawn. White gets a half-open c-file against the c7 pawn, and Black's usual recapture, ...exd5, puts a pawn on d5 that blocks the long diagonal for the b7-bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 d5 5.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6 knight at once and keeps the choice of exchanging on d5 for later, so Black must commit first. A flexible move that heads for a calm game with the tension in the centre intact.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 d5 5.e3.strategy: A solid developing move that supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop. White keeps a healthy pawn structure and heads for a patient middlegame, but does little to make Black's b6 advance a liability.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6 4.Nc3 d5 5.cxd.strategy: Recaptures with the e-pawn, which keeps a pawn on d5 and opens the e-file against e2. The planned b7-bishop is blunted by its own pawn, so Black must find play elsewhere, but the structure is solid.

Takes with the knight, which keeps the e-pawn at home and the long diagonal open for the bishop that will come to b7. The price is that White can gain central space by attacking the knight with a pawn, so Black must be ready to meet a broad pawn centre.
Loses the queen: the knight on c3 takes it, and Black gets only a knight and a pawn in return.
Pins the f6 knight against the queen at once, while Black has not yet developed the rest of the pieces. Black has to spend a move to unravel the pin, and White keeps the pressure on d5 and e4.
Supports d4 and frees the f1-bishop for calm development. White keeps a sound pawn structure and plays a patient game against a set-up in which Black's b6 pawn and bishop have little to do.
Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, where it eyes c7 and the d6 square. It gives up the pressure on the f6 knight that Bg5 would keep, so Black can finish development without difficulty.

Answers the pin by developing the bishop behind the knight and preparing to castle. Black keeps a solid position with a pawn on d5 against White's pressure, though the pieces stay somewhat passive until they find squares.
Develops the bishop and adds a defender to d5, so the pawn holds even if White trades on f6. But the bishop is blocked by its own pawn and the knight stays pinned for now, so Black remains passive.
Backs d5 with a pawn, a solid way to keep the centre. It costs the knight the c6 square and leaves the f6 knight pinned, so White can trade it off; a quiet game in which Black has no active play yet.
